title: Lists, Dictionaries, and Tuples
summary: Store ordered sequences in lists, map keys to values in dictionaries, and group fixed records in immutable tuples.

steps.title: Ordered, mutable sequences
steps.lede: A list stores an ordered sequence of values you can index, slice and modify.

blocks.text: Keeping five separate variables for five delivery times gets unwieldy fast. A list stores an ordered sequence of values in a single name: delivery_times = [32, 45, 21, 60, 18]. Items are indexed from 0 at the left and from -1 at the right, so delivery_times[0] is 32 and delivery_times[-1] is 18.

A slice extracts a sub-list: delivery_times[1:3] returns [45, 21]. The start index is included; the end index is excluded. delivery_times[-3:] returns the last three items. Lists are mutable: delivery_times[3] = 64 replaces the item at index 3 in place.

steps.title: Modify and extend a list
steps.lede: Can you predict what a list looks like after an assignment and an append?

public.prompt:
After running:

```python
delivery_times = [32, 45, 21]
delivery_times[1] = 50
delivery_times.append(18)
```

What is the value of `delivery_times`?

opt_a.message: Correct. `delivery_times[1] = 50` replaces the item at index 1 (which was `45`) with `50`, and `.append(18)` adds `18` at the end.

opt_b.message: The assignment `delivery_times[1] = 50` replaces the item at index 1. Index 1 holds `45`, so after the assignment it becomes `50`, not `45`.

opt_c.message: Index 1 is the second item (`45`), not the first (`32`). `delivery_times[1] = 50` replaces `45` with `50`, leaving `32` unchanged.

opt_d.message: `.append(18)` adds `18` to the end of the list. The list should have four items after both operations.

correct.message: Right — `delivery_times[1] = 50` replaces the item at index 1 (was `45`, now `50`), and `.append(18)` adds `18` at the end: `[32, 50, 21, 18]`.

incorrect.message: Index 1 is the second item. `delivery_times[1] = 50` replaces `45` with `50`. Then `.append(18)` adds `18` at the end.

hints: List indexes start at 0. What item is at index 1 in `[32, 45, 21]`?
`.append(value)` always adds to the end. How many items does the list have after both operations?

steps.title: Key-to-value lookup
steps.lede: A dictionary maps unique keys to values — look up a city by order ID, not by position.

blocks.text: Sometimes you need to look up a value by a meaningful key rather than by position. A dictionary is a collection of key: value pairs written inside braces, where keys must be unique: order_city = {1042: 'Lagos', 1043: 'Abuja', 1044: 'Kano'}. Retrieve a value by subscripting with its key: order_city[1042] returns 'Lagos'.

Store or update a value by assigning to a key: order_city[1044] = 'Kano' adds a new entry; assigning to an existing key replaces its value. The get() method returns None (or a specified default) instead of raising an error when a key is absent: order_city.get(9999) returns None rather than crashing.
Subscripting a key that is not in the dictionary raises a KeyError: order_city[9999] fails if no order 9999 was ever added. Use get() when you are not certain the key exists.

steps.title: Predict what happens with a missing key
steps.lede: What does Python do when you subscript a key that is not in the dictionary?

public.prompt:
After running:

```python
order_city = {1042: 'Lagos', 1043: 'Abuja'}
print(order_city[1099])
```

What happens?

options.text: Raises a `KeyError` — key `1099` is not in the dictionary
Prints `None` — Python returns `None` for missing keys
Prints an empty string — Python returns `''` for missing keys
Raises a `ValueError` — the key type does not match

opt_a.message: Correct. Subscripting a dictionary with a key that does not exist raises `KeyError`. Use `.get()` if you want `None` instead of an error.

opt_b.message: Subscripting with `[]` raises `KeyError` for a missing key. To get `None` for a missing key, use `order_city.get(1099)` instead.

opt_c.message: Python does not return an empty string for missing keys. Subscripting with `[]` raises `KeyError`; use `.get()` to get a default value.

opt_d.message: The error is `KeyError`, not `ValueError`. Python raises `KeyError` when the key is not present, regardless of the key's type.

correct.message: Right — `order_city[1099]` raises `KeyError` because `1099` is not a key in the dictionary. Use `.get(1099)` to get `None` instead of an error.

incorrect.message: Subscripting a dictionary with a missing key raises `KeyError`. To avoid the error, use `.get(key)` which returns `None` (or a default) when the key is absent.

hints: What does Python do when you use `d[key]` and `key` is not in `d`?
Which method returns `None` instead of raising an error for a missing key?

steps.title: Immutable sequences and unpacking
steps.lede: A tuple groups a fixed set of values; unpacking hands each piece back to its own name.

blocks.text: A tuple groups a small, fixed set of values together. It is written as comma-separated values, with or without surrounding parentheses: order = 1042, 'Lagos', 32 or order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32). Python shows tuples enclosed in parentheses on output.

Tuples are immutable: once created, an item cannot be reassigned. order[0] = 1099 raises a TypeError. Also, enclosing a single value in parentheses does not make it a tuple — singleton = ('Lagos') is still just the string 'Lagos'. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: singleton = 'Lagos',

annotations.text: Three values packed into one tuple

blocks.change_summary: Unpacking hands each element of the tuple back to its own name — order_id, city and minutes are now separate variables.

steps.title: Recognise when a one-item tuple needs a trailing comma
steps.lede: Which expression actually creates a tuple with one element?

public.prompt: Which of the following creates a **tuple** containing the single value `'Lagos'`?

opt_a.message: Correct. A trailing comma after the value creates a one-item tuple: `'Lagos',` is a tuple. The parentheses are optional.

opt_b.message: `('Lagos')` is just `'Lagos'` in parentheses — the parentheses are grouping, not a tuple. Without a trailing comma, Python sees a plain string.

opt_c.message: `['Lagos']` creates a **list** with one item, not a tuple. Lists use square brackets; tuples use commas (with optional parentheses).

opt_d.message: `{'Lagos'}` creates a **set** with one item, not a tuple. Sets use curly braces; tuples use commas.

correct.message: Right — a one-item tuple requires a trailing comma: `'Lagos',` or `('Lagos',)`. Without the comma, `('Lagos')` is just a string in parentheses.

incorrect.message: A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `singleton = 'Lagos',`. Without the comma, parentheses alone do not create a tuple.

hints: What makes a tuple a tuple — the parentheses, or the commas?
Try `type(('Lagos'))` versus `type(('Lagos',))` — what does each return?

blocks.text: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence indexed from 0; slices use start-included, end-excluded bounds; index assignment replaces an item in place and append() adds one at the end. A dictionary maps unique keys to values; subscripting a missing key raises a KeyError — use get() to avoid it. A tuple groups a fixed set of values that cannot be reassigned; unpacking distributes each element to its own name.

blocks.text: Lists are mutable: you can replace any item by assigning to its index. delivery_times[3] = 64 changes the value at index 3 in place. append() adds a new item to the end: delivery_times.append(27) grows the list by one.

blocks.change_summary: Index assignment replaces an item in place; append() adds a new item at the end.

blocks.text: Subscripting a key that is not in the dictionary raises a KeyError. order_city[9999] fails if 9999 was never added. Use get() to avoid the error: order_city.get(9999) returns None instead of crashing.

blocks.takeaway: Use get() when you are not certain the key exists; it returns None (or a default) instead of raising an error.

remediation_steps.title: One-item tuples need a trailing comma
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing that parentheses alone do not create a tuple.

blocks.text: Enclosing a single value in parentheses does not make it a tuple — singleton = ('Lagos') is still just the string 'Lagos'. A one-item tuple requires a trailing comma: singleton = 'Lagos', or equivalently singleton = ('Lagos',).

blocks.takeaway: The trailing comma, not the parentheses, is what makes a one-item tuple.
